query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A pre-treatment that refines the grain structure and boosts the density of twins in the FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating promotes the formation of a stable twin‐enhanced subsurface during high‐temperature sliding. This dynamic twin network impedes dislocation motion and delays surface softening, thereby limiting plastic deformation and reducing wear rate.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coating with a relatively coarse grain structure and moderate intrinsic twin density
generation.intervention: Apply a post-deposition heat treatment/process that refines the grain size and increases pre-existing twin densities before subjecting the coating to sliding wear tests
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests in a high-temperature regime (e.g., around 400°C and above) under controlled load and sliding speed that simulate the intended operating conditions
generation.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with enhanced twin boundaries that serve as barriers to dislocation slip
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature sliding, the refined, twin-rich microstructure dynamically forms and maintains a subsurface layer where twin boundaries block dislocation motion and dissipate frictional energy. This minimizes plastic flow and adhesive interactions at the interface, reducing wear damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline (as-deposited) coating, the heat-treated, grain-refined coating should exhibit a lower wear rate, reduced friction coefficient, and less pronounced microscopic plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding tests.
generation.baseline: Standard as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without a grain-refining/twin-enhancing post-treatment
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to govern the wear behavior when frictional heat is significant (≥400°C) and before other high-temperature degradation processes (e.g., extensive oxidation) dominate. Its benefit might be reduced if the coating microstructure coarsens or if compositional factors (such as varying Cu levels) alter the twin formation dynamics.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extrapolates the influence of twin formation on wear resistance observed in related HEA systems (as reported in PMC10058552’s conclusions and PMC10241162’s evidence on adaptive friction interface protection) to the specific FeNiCrCoCu coating. Uncertainty remains regarding the precise quantitative relationship between twin density and wear performance in this alloy, and how compositional variations might also play a role.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on the same conventional metal substrate. One set remains in the as-deposited state (baseline) while the second set undergoes a controlled heat treatment aimed at refining grain size and promoting twin formation. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under high-temperature conditions (around 400°C) at fixed load and sliding speed. Post-test, use SEM, TEM/EBSD and nanoindentation to assess wear loss, friction coefficient, and subsurface microstructural features (grain/twin density).
measurements: Wear loss (mass loss or volume loss)
Grain size and twin density assessment via TEM or EBSD
Surface and subsurface morphology via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated (grain-refined) coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction coefficient compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal an increased density of twin boundaries in the subsurface region during or after high-temperature sliding, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In addition, the tensile and compression property of polycrystalline HEA with larger particle sizes is not as good as HEA with smaller particle sizes. This is attributed to the obstruction of grain boundaries and the degree of dislocation entanglement when dislocations cross grain boundaries in polycrystalline HEAs. In addition, due to the presence of grain boundaries, the stress of polycrystalline HEAs does not decrease rapidly after reaching tensile and compression limits. Finally, at 300 K, tensile and compressive loads are applied to pure nickel and nickel coated with FeNiCrCoCu HEAs. The results show that the microscopic mechanism of HEAs strengthening nickel is that the climb of dislocations in HEAs promotes the formation of twins in nickel, thereby improving the strength of nickel. After HEAs coating strengthening, the tensile-compression asymmetry of nickel was reduced by 18%. This is due to twin degradation due to the different atomic sizes of the main elements of HEA.

cited_evidence.text: No micro-pits or debris are observed from the Ni3X surface away from the worn track (Fig. S9), confirming that they are indeed generated during sliding. For NiX, its worn track dimensions also increase at 400 °C compared to those at RT, but the worn surface remains relatively smooth and is free of debris and micro-pits (Fig. S7b). This uncovers that NiX still outperforms Ni3X in resisting the elastic–plastic deformation involved with abrasive wear even at 400 °C. The higher high-temperature hardness of NiX may be responsible for the low wear rate compared to Ni3X at 400 °C (Fig. 3A). Nanoindentation tests (Fig. S2) also show that H on the worn surface of NiX (5.9 GPa) at 400 °C is higher than that of Ni3X (4.9 GPa).
